# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–5 (Complete and Final – Updated 67)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; nearly three weeks into new year (1832) just after Lords threw out Reform Bill; summer and autumn of first year; winter of first year; Vauxhall evening during spring of first year; spring of second year; narrative extends into future years; present day with Fred and Mary at Stone Court in white-haired placidity
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring, Wilhaven, Salford, Chiswick Mall, Hammersmith, Soho, Thames, England, Oxford, Chiswick Church, Buxton, Kensington turnpike, Russell Square, London, Southampton Row, Vauxhall, Exeter 'Change, India (Boggley Wollah, Ramgunge, Budgebudge, Calcutta, Dumdum), Forty Thieves theatre, King's 14th regiment post, Highbury Barn, Covent Garden Market, Doctor Swishtail's Seminary, Bedford tavern, Thames Street (City), Royal Gardens, Quenwick (harbor town), Wilhaven (harbor town), St. George's Hanover Square, Lambeth Palace, Cheltenham, Great Gaunt Street, Queen's Crawley (Hants), Mudbury, Gaunt Square, Mansion House, Oxford Street, Swallow Street, Cambridge
- **Environmental Details**: Rain threatening; wind from water with salt and tar smell; gulls quarreling; smoke from chimneys lying flat over fields; frost silvering hedges; light going early; children chasing hoop down lane; road all ruts and puddles after thaw; dog barked then went quiet; river up in spring; muddy square; roseate summer morning making Great Gaunt Street look cheerful; leather doors at 'Necks

## Main Characters

**Dorothea and Will Ladislaw (Married)**
- Engaged after Will's return; now married with infant son; established pattern of two yearly visits to Grange; Dorothea's life mixed result of young, noble impulse; finely touched spirit with fine issues though not widely visible; full nature spent in channels with no great name; effect incalculably diffusive

**Mary Garth and Fred Garth (Married)**
- Inhabit Stone Court; seen in white-haired placidity at open window; solid mutual happiness; Fred becomes distinguished county farmer; produces work on "Cultivation of Green Crops and the Economy of Cattle-Feeding" winning agricultural meeting congratulations; Fred gradually saved enough to become Stone Court owner; three boys only, youngest resembles grandfather

**Rebecca Sharp (Miss Becky)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Age and Background**: Age nineteen; father was artist/drawing teacher at Miss Pinkerton's academy—clever, prone to debt and tavern, beat wife and daughter when drunk, died after third delirium tremens; mother was French opera-girl; claims descent from noble Entrechats family of Gascony; had dismal precocity of poverty
- **Appearance**: Small, slight, pale, sandy-haired with large, odd, attractive eyes; white slender fingers
- **Accomplishments**: Speaks French with purity and Parisian accent; skilled musician and linguist; clever artist; sings better than Amelia
- **Departure from Chiswick**: Threw Dixonary at Miss Jemima; obtained governess position with Sir Pitt Crawley's family; Miss Pinkerton recommended her: "I cannot find fault with Miss Sharp's conduct except to myself; must allow her talents and accomplishments are of high order"
- **Calculated Nature**: Determined to make connected plans for future; never blushed since age eight when caught stealing jam; capable of calculated charm and intimacy
- **Joseph Sedley Romance Campaign**: Upon learning of Joseph Sedley's wealth, determined "If Mr. Joseph Sedley is rich and unmarried, why should I not marry him?"; invited by Amelia; won over entire household through charming behavior; left alone with Joseph in drawing-room; occupied knitting green silk purse; established great confidence and intimacy; Joseph began eloquent speech "O Miss Sharp, how--" but stopped when music ended; continued presenting nosegays; Rebecca refused his request to sing citing low spirits; asked him to help finish green silk purse; Joseph seated tete-a-tete with killing expression, hands bound in green silk web; Rebecca thought "I might go farther, and fare worse"
- **At Vauxhall**: Took Jos's arm; sat by him on open carriage box; everyone expected marriage announcement; lost themselves in solitary walk among couples; at Moscow panorama, rude fellow treading on foot caused her to fall into Joseph's arms; Joseph told favorite Indian stories again (sixth time); at supper during inebriation, Jos clasped her round waist shouting "Stop, my dearest diddle-diddle-darling"; Rebecca started but could not get away hand
- **After Vauxhall - Rejection and Departure**: Spent day observing from second-floor bedroom watching for Joseph; began feeling distrust and hatred toward George Osborne after he laughed at her; feared Osborne had frightened Joseph away; Jos never came; received Jos's letter announcing departure to Cheltenham and Scotland; household turned against Rebecca; Blenkinsop reported Rebecca reading Mrs. Sedley's letters and accessing trinket boxes; Pinner suspected Rebecca had taken Amelia's white ribbing; entire household (except Amelia) agreed Rebecca should depart speedily
- **Departure from Sedley Household**: Accepted Amelia's generous presents with proper hesitation; received purse from Mr. Sedley; kissed his hand, asked to consider him kind protector; behavior affecting—Mr. Sedley blessed her, invited her to always come when in town; parting with Amelia theatrical—one person earnest, other perfect performer; after tenderest caresses, pathetic tears, smelling-bottle; Rebecca vowed to love Amelia forever; Amelia wept on Blenkinsop's shoulder
- **New Position - Governess at Crawley**: Immediately upon departure counted guineas and began planning; contemplated what Baronet must be, wondered if he wore star, imagined him court-suited like Mr. Wroughton; expected contemptuously treated but thought "at least, I shall be amongst GENTLEFOLKS, and not with vulgar city people"; fell thinking of Russell Square friends with philosophical bitterness; carriage passed through Gaunt Square into Great Gaunt Street, stopped at tall gloomy house between two others with hatchment over middle drawing-room window
- **Arrival at Crawley's Great Gaunt Street House**: Door opened by man in drab breeches, gaiters, dirty coat, foul neckcloth, shining bald head, leering red face, twinkling grey eyes, perpetually grinning mouth; John the groom (attached to lady's maid) called Rebecca "a bad lot" and said she had robbed the maid of perquisites (Amelia's gowns intended as lady's maid's)
- **First Evening at Crawley House**: Found dining-room cheerless—chambers mourning absence of masters; turkey carpet rolled up under sideboard; pictures hidden behind brown paper; ceiling lamp muffled in brown holland; window-curtains disappeared; marble bust of Sir Walpole Crawley in black corner; card-racks empty; cellaret hidden; chairs turned up along walls; old-fashioned locked knife-box on dumb waiter. Sir Pitt extracted tripe and onion from saucepan, divided portions with Mrs. Tinker (on board wages when he absent, dines with family when in town); told Rebecca he's glad she's not hungry
- **Sir Pitt's Confidences**: Discussed numerous lawsuits—"Crawley, Bart. v. Snaffle," "Podder and another versus Crawley, Bart.," "Overseers of Snaily parish against Crawley, Bart."—claiming common land belongs to him not parish; willing to spend thousand guineas to win; asked Rebecca to write good hand, said he'd make her useful at Queen's Crawley now dowager dead; talked incessantly in coarsest Hampshire accent and man-of-the-world tone; called late wife "close" but "valuable woman" who saved him steward; injected Rebecca be ready at five in morning
- **First Night**: Instructed Rebecca sleep with Tinker, said "it's a big bed, and there's room for two. Lady Crawley died in it"; Tinker, with rushlight, led Rebecca past muffled drawing-room door handles into great front bedroom where Lady Crawley slept her last; bed and chamber so funereal, seemed Lady Crawley's ghost inhabited it; Rebecca sprang about with greatest liveliness, peeped into huge wardrobes, closets, cupboards, tried locked drawers, examined dreary pictures and toilette appointments while Tinker said prayers; old charwoman said "I shouldn't like to sleep in this yeer bed without a good conscience, Miss"; Rebecca replied "There's room for us and a half-dozen of ghosts in it"; pumped Tinker for information about Lady Crawley and Sir Pitt but Tinker signified bed for sleeping not conversation and produced snore only innocent nose can produce; Rebecca lay awake long time thinking of morrow and new world, chances of success; rushlight flickered; mantelpiece cast black shadow over mouldy old sampler worked by deceased ladyship and two family pictures—one young lad in college gown, other in red soldier jacket; Rebecca dreamed of soldier picture
- **Departure Morning**: At four o'clock on roseate summer morning, Tinker wakened Rebecca, bid her prepare; unbarred and unbolted great hall door (clanging startled echoes), took way to Oxford Street, summoned coach from stand; driver hoped for young buck from tavern; Sir Pitt did not give one penny more than fare; driver flung Miss Sharp's bandboxes in gutter at 'Necks, swore he'd take law against fare; Sir Pitt told coachman "Keep the box for me, Leader"; coachman replied "Yes, Sir Pitt" with rage in soul (promised box to young Cambridge gentleman who would have given crown); Rebecca accommodated with back seat inside carriage carrying her into wide world
- **Letter to Amelia**: Rebecca wrote pathetic letter describing fatal night of separation, tears and sadness; mentioned Amelia went Tuesday to joy and happiness with mother and devoted young soldier by side, dancing at Perkins's Ball, prettiest young lady; Rebecca brought by groom in old carriage to Sir Pitt's town house; after John the groom behaved rudely and insolently; given to Sir P.'s care; made to pass night in old gloomy bed by horrid charwoman keeping house; did not sleep one wink whole night

**Joseph Sedley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Position and Background**: In East India Company's Civil Service; collector of Boggley Wollah for about eight years; caught liver complaint, returned to Europe; has own lodgings, not with family
- **Appearance and Habits**: Very stout, puffy man in buckskins and Hessian boots with immense neckcloths, red striped waistcoat, apple green coat with steel buttons; drives horses in Park, dines at fashionable taverns, frequents theatres and opera; extremely talkative in man's society
- **At Vauxhall**: Escorted Rebecca to dinner and gardens; at supper ordered waiters with majesty, made salad, uncorked Champagne, carved chickens, ate greater part of refreshments; insisted bowl of rack punch, drank entire contents; became inebriated, talked and laughed loudly, voluntarily sang in maudlin high key, became bold as lion, clasped Rebecca round waist shouting "Stop, my dearest diddle-diddle-darling"; continued drinking, making love, singing
- **Post-Vauxhall Crisis**: George Osborne pushed Jos back into seat; Jos kissed hand to retreating ladies hiccupping "Bless you!"; seized Dobbin's hand weeping, confided he adored Rebecca, broke her heart, would marry her next morning; Dobbin shrewdly induced him to leave, conveyed him home; next morning Jos groaned in severe agonies; George Osborne found him groaning on sofa; Dobbin already in room tending patient; Jos's valet Mr. Brush reported Jos "uncommon wild," wanted fight hackney-coachman, Captain brought him upstairs like baby
- **Escape and Flight**: Osborne mercilessly mocked Jos about Vauxhall behavior, called him milksop, mocked maudlin state, ridicule about "my dearest diddle-diddle-darling"; sent letter to Amelia apologizing for Vauxhall conduct, attributing to rack punch, announcing immediate departure for Cheltenham and later Scotland for several months; thus avoided formal proposal entirely; Jos fled town, leaving Rebecca's hopes dashed
- **Father's Assessment**: Old Mr. Sedley feels akin to contempt for son; says Joseph vain, selfish, lazy, effeminate; sure Joseph would say "Good Gad!" and eat dinner if family died; not anxious about him

**Miss Amelia Sedley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Character**: Pupil at Miss Pinkerton's; happy, handsome, seventeen years old; loves Rebecca like sister; natural infirmity of tears; match-maker at heart; too good, too kind, doesn't know world
- **Betrothal**: Bred up for purpose of marrying George Osborne; banns read in respective families for ten years; appeared to fall in love with George at single instant when he asked her for music
- **Regarding Rebecca and Vauxhall Aftermath**: Discovered million of virtues in Rebecca; warmed into most tender friendship; showed her rooms, books, piano, dresses, necklaces, braces, laces; insisted Rebecca accept white cornelian and turquoise rings, sprigged muslin, white Cashmere shawl; entirely agreed with mother's changed opinion; thought Jos must propose next day; sent page to Jos's lodgings; reply through Mr. Brush that master was ill in bed with doctor; believed he must come to-morrow but never had courage to speak to Rebecca; looked reprovingly at George when he laughed at Rebecca; after Jos left town, never had further word from him
- **Parting with Rebecca**: Ransacked all drawers, cupboards, reticules, gimcrack boxes to select presents; went to Papa to beg he give his promised money (as many guineas as she was years old) to Rebecca instead; wept confidentially on Blenkinsop's shoulder about household suspicions; parting theatrical scene—one person earnest, other perfect performer; after tenderest caresses and pathetic tears with smelling-bottle; vowed to love Rebecca forever; received pathetic letter from Rebecca describing her arrival at Sir Pitt's

**George Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Background**: Sedley's godson; family friend for twenty-three years; clever artist; bred up for purpose of marrying Amelia
- **At Vauxhall**: Paired with Amelia; at supper in mated pair; did not like rack punch; intervened with commotion, single push sent Jos back into seat; removed ladies in safety
- **Post-Vauxhall Campaign Against Rebecca-Jos Match**: Found Jos groaning next morning; not pleased that family member into which he was marrying should make mesalliance with little nobody—little upstart governess; pursued advantage pitilessly; thought Jos milksop; mocked Jos relentlessly about behavior and romantic declarations; inspired distrust and hatred in Rebecca; laughed at her discomfited mien; when Rebecca came downstairs, continued liveliness and banter; told Amelia she must learn her station, called her helpless creature; said Amelia too good, too kind, doesn't know world; expressed manly compunction for unnecessary unkindness; his mockery and interference effectively discouraged Jos from pursuing proposal

**William Dobbin** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Background**: Son of merchant/grocer; father keeps shop "Figs & Rudge" on Thames Street, City; father became Alderman Dobbin, Colonel of City Light Horse, later knighted; Dobbin entered army
- **School Experience**: Giant amongst boys at Doctor Swishtail's Seminary, mercilessly bullied; defended George Osborne by fighting Cuff; thirteen-round left-handed fight, eventually prevailed; character rose prodigiously in estimation; name "Figs" became respectable and popular
- **At Vauxhall and Post-Vauxhall**: Asked by George to look after shawls; carried Amelia's white cashmere shawl; paid at door for whole party; found himself humming Amelia's tune she sang on stairs; realized he was forgotten, decided he would be de trop; walked away; while walking about gardens, stepped up to supper box in agitated state when commotion seemed inevitable; shouldered off crowd
- **Jos's Departure**: Jos seized Dobbin's hand and confided secret of his loves; Dobbin shrewdly induced him to leave gardens and hastened him to Lambeth Palace; conveyed Jos into hackney-coach depositing him at lodgings; next morning found Jos groaning on sofa, good-naturedly tended patient; entreated Osborne to have mercy when he mocked Jos
- **Emotional Attachment**: Found himself unconsciously humming Amelia's tune; emotional attachment to Amelia beginning to develop

**Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Background and Ancestry**: Named after the great Commoner; son of Walpole Crawley, first Baronet, of Tape and Sealing-Wax Office in reign of George II (impeached for peculation); family tree includes John Churchill Crawley, Charles Stuart Barebones Crawley, Queen Elizabeth's Crawley (forked beard, armour)
- **Marriages and Children**: First married to Grizzel, sixth daughter of Mungo Binkie, Lord Binkie (cousin of Mr. Dundas); she brought two sons—Pitt (named after minister) and Rawdon Crawley (named from Prince of Wales's friend); many years after Grizzel's demise, Sir Pitt led Rosa, daughter of Mr. G. Dawson of Mudbury, to altar; by Rosa he had two daughters for whom Rebecca Sharp now engaged as governess
- **Estate and Borough**: Owner of Queen's Crawley estate in Hants and Great Gaunt Street mansion in London; Queen's Crawley formerly erected by Queen Elizabeth after she was delighted with Hampshire beer; now "rotten borough" producing "good fifteen hundred a year"; family represented in Parliament constantly
- **Appearance**: Man in drab breeches and gaiters, dirty old coat, foul old neckcloth, shining bald head, leering red face, twinkling grey eyes, mouth perpetually on grin
- **Character and Behavior**: Talkative, incessantly discussing himself; sometimes coarsest and vulgarest Hampshire accent, sometimes man-of-the-world tone; does not disguise his qualities
- **Lawsuits**: Involved in numerous cases—"Crawley, Bart. v. Snaffle" (plans to throw Snaffle over), "Podder and another versus Crawley, Bart.," "Overseers of Snaily parish against Crawley, Bart." (claims common land belongs to him not parish, willing to spend thousand guineas to win)
- **Wife (Rosa) - Deceased**: Called by Sir Pitt "the dowager" and "Lady Crawley"; was close but valuable woman who saved him steward; had mouldy old sampler in bedroom; had two little family pictures (young lads in college gown and red soldier jacket); slept in great front bedroom of Great Gaunt Street house; now dead (timing unclear—at least some time ago as Sir Pitt seeking replacement help)
- **Plans for Rebecca**: Now dowager dead, wants someone (Rebecca) to be useful at Queen's Crawley; plans to have her write good hand, help with documents

**Mrs. Tinker (Old Charwoman)**
- Keeps Sir Pitt's Great Gaunt Street house; on board wages when Sir Pitt absent, dines with family when in town; shared supper of tripe and onion with Sir Pitt; sleeps with rushlight; leads Rebecca through house; said prayers before bed; would not be pumped by Rebecca for information; only snored in response to questions, signifying bed for sleeping not conversation; snore only innocence can produce

## Minor Characters Referenced
- John the groom (attached to lady's maid, called Rebecca "bad lot"); Mazek, Aessa, Ulvie Hollwood, Halan, Elnar, Jotho Corrett, Cotho Brackwood, Senelle Brackwood (died from fall from mill loft, buried at Fenmere), Tassa Brackwood, Cotho Brackwood (complained of aching back), Leader the coachman, Mr. Brush (Jos's valet), Blenkinsop (Mrs. Sedley's maid), Pinner, Miss Jemima Pinkerton

## Critical Facts and Status
- Rebecca departed London by coach early morning with bandboxes; received back seat inside carriage; on way to Queen's Crawley estate in Hants; wrote pathetic letter to Amelia; Sir Pitt planning to employ her usefulness at Queen's Crawley; her governessing duties with Sir Pitt's two daughters about to commence
